overview: These medieval “Berbers” and “Berber tribes” labels cover a broad western Saharan area, not one kingdom or all Amazigh peoples. Named communities and trading towns had their own histories. The outline does not establish ethnic or modern political boundaries. Medieval evidence below is followed by explicitly dated examples of continuing regional knowledge and language.

periods.title: Trading towns in the earlier map window
periods.summary: Tegdaoust expanded during the tenth century, joining local crafts to commerce across the Sahara.

periods.title: Almoravid power
periods.summary: A dynasty with Saharan roots ruled in Morocco and parts of Spain between the two imported map windows.

periods.title: The later cultural label
periods.summary: The map’s second label is a regional generalization, not evidence of a new founding or collective disappearance.

periods.title: A modern written voice
periods.summary: A preschool booklet and subsequent educational research document Amazigh writing for young learners in Morocco.

items.text: The Almoravid movement arose among Sanhaja groups including the Lamtuna and Gudala in the Mauritanian Adrar. It grew into a major power in Morocco and Spain. This is one influential political story within the region, while other communities followed different paths.

Azougui preserves occupation reaching at least the eleventh century. New research makes an important distinction: the visible fortified enclosure once called an Almoravid fortress belongs to a later period. Archaeology can change a famous monument’s date while leaving the wider town’s medieval history intact.

Tegdaoust, usually identified with medieval Awdaghost, expanded in the early tenth century. An organized pattern of urban plots took shape, and houses developed within it over succeeding centuries. Wells helped support this trading settlement in the western Saharan landscape.

Tegdaoust craftspeople worked copper and iron and made pottery by hand. Excavated glass and wheel-made ceramics point to imports from north of the Sahara. The town connected local production to the redistribution of goods over long distances.

A Mauritanian heritage description from 2001 records Azougui’s date-palm oasis, irrigation channels and festivities linked to the date season. Cultivating an oasis involved skilled water management as well as harvesting fruit; its working landscape also carried community memories.

A 2025 UNESCO account describes Amazigh village assemblies in southern Morocco temporarily closing pastures, forests or orchards to use. This Agdal system gives resources time to recover. Deciding when everyone can harvest is part of the practical work of living together.

The same report describes Tanast irrigation timing: a pierced copper bowl floats in water until it fills and sinks. Families with water rights receive allotted numbers of these time units. A sinking bowl can therefore help decide when it is the next field’s turn.

sections.title: Homes and food in later regional examples

items.text: A tent collected at Tiidrine in Morocco in 1983 was made from long strips of woven goat hair sewn together. Its preserved equipment includes spare cloth, yarn and large needles. A portable home still needed maintenance, and this one came with a repair kit.

UNESCO’s 2014 account describes argan-oil makers harvesting and processing fruit, using a hand mill and carefully adding warm water. Women teach the skills to their daughters; oil also appears in wedding gifts and festive cooking. This connects household knowledge, craft tools and celebration.

sections.title: Learning and a written language sample

items.text: An Amazigh-language literacy programme for argan cooperatives began in December 2008. UNESCO’s 2015 report describes lessons using DVDs, discussion and group work. Women studied subjects including accounting, oil quality and family law through language they already used in daily life.

That programme also learned to fit school around family work. An early, abundant harvest drew some women away from lessons, so organizers changed timetables and arranged catch-up opportunities. A good harvest should not have to mean the end of learning.

“ⴰⵣⵓⵍ ⴰ ⵉⵎⵥⵢⴰⵏⵏ !” (azul a imẓyann!) means “Hello, little ones!” It is the title of a 2007 preschool booklet, documented by Morocco’s Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture. This modern Tifinagh sample greeted children aged four to six; it is not a medieval quotation.

ending.text: The map’s 1279 endpoint is a data boundary, not an ending for these peoples. Political authorities, settlement patterns and languages changed over time. The dated modern examples show Amazigh communities continuing to teach, organize, make things and manage shared resources.
